nameStory: The 'large twayblade' name comes from its pair of broad leaves - 'tway' is an old English word meaning 'two,' and 'blade' refers to the leaf shape. It's called 'large' to distinguish it from smaller twayblade orchids, though at just a few inches tall, it's still quite petite by most plant standards!
description: Large twayblade is a delicate native orchid that grows just 4-8 inches tall from the forest floor. It features two broad, oval leaves that clasp around the stem near the base, and a slender spike of small purplish-brown flowers above. This little orchid is much more subtle than the showy orchids you might see in a florist shop, with flowers that blend beautifully into the woodland shadows.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two broad, oval leaves that feel smooth and somewhat succulent, positioned opposite each other partway up the stem and wrapping around it like they're giving it a gentle hug

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purplish-brown to mauve flowers arranged in a loose cluster atop the stem, each flower has a distinctive wide lower lip that gives the plant its 'widelip orchid' nickname

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single slender stem rising 4-8 inches from the ground, often appearing alone or in small scattered groups rather than dense colonies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, oval seed capsules that split open to release dust-like seeds - the capsules feel papery and dry when mature

habitat: Look for large twayblade in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests, often on slopes or in woodland clearings with dappled sunlight. It prefers well-drained but consistently moist soil with plenty of organic matter, and you'll often find it among ferns, wild ginger, and other shade-loving woodland plants.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring as two tightly rolled leaves that gradually unfurl and expand through May.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from late June through July, followed by developing seed capsules through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and wither by September, and seed capsules mature and split open to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, existing only as underground structures until the following spring.

funFact: Like many orchids, large twayblade has a secret partnership with underground fungi that help feed the plant - without these fungal allies, the dust-like seeds (which are smaller than grains of salt) couldn't grow into new plants!
confusionNotes: The two-leaved arrangement might remind you of trout lily or other woodland plants, but large twayblade's leaves clasp around the stem rather than emerging separately from the ground, and only orchids produce that distinctive three-petaled flower structure with the prominent lower lip.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'large' twayblade, this orchid is actually quite small and easily overlooked - the name only makes sense when comparing it to its even tinier relative, the fen orchid, which has much narrower leaves and grows in wetlands.
compareHints: Large twayblade differs from its close relative fen orchid by having much broader, oval leaves (fen orchid has narrow, lance-shaped leaves) and preferring rich forest soils rather than wetlands. The flowers of large twayblade are also more purple-brown while fen orchid flowers tend to be more yellowish-green.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fen orchid differs from its relative large twayblade by being much smaller overall and having distinctly yellowish-green flowers rather than purplish-brown ones.
